newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress polls may galvanise party.
newsitem.headline: India Congress polls may galvanise party.

text.p: A bitter contest to select a new head for India's Congress party is unlikely to split the nation's oldest political bloc and might even rejuvenate it, leaders and analysts said on Thursday.
"I don't think there will be a split," said Rajesh Pilot, one of the three contestants in the race for Congress presidentship.
"We are all party workers, we are fighting elections within the party," Pilot told Reuters.
Pilot is pitted against party chief Sitaram Kesri, 76, and Sharad Pawar, a party heavyweight from the most-industrialised western state of Maharashtra.

Congress provides key support to the ruling United Front, and Kesri has received flak from his colleagues for suddenly withdrawing that support last April and renewing it only after the coalition replaced H.D. Deve Gowda as prime minister.
However, Kesri's supporters say both Pawar and Pilot have failed to elicit the support of the delegates.
Nearly 8,000 party delegates are slated to vote in the elections set for June 9 and results would be known by June 12.
If the candidates are unable to bury their differences and arrive at a consensus, it will be only the third set of internal elections in the 112-year history of the Congress party, officials said.
Congress has ruled India for all but five years since independence from Britain in 1947, but has been hit by a string of scandals and suffered a crushing loss in general elections last year.
It provides vital support to Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's ruling coalition.
"I don't think the Congress will be split. They have nowhere to go," said B. G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research. "Who will accept them."
Verghese said the elections instead would strengthen the party and was a healthy development.
Pawar and Pilot have repeatedly attacked Kesri, accusing him of manipulating the organisational elections.
News reports quoted Pawar as saying that his candidature was aimed at bringing in collective leadership that the party now lacked and delegate decision making to lower officials.
"There is hell of a lot of silent support," said Pilot. "I am confident we will achieve our goal."
Senior party leader Ved Prakash said there was overwhelming support for Kesri and the other two contestants were preparing the ground for the future.
Elections for party leader are held every two years.
"The party will be galvanised, the aim is to revitalise the party," Ved Prakash said. "Nobody wants the Congress to become weak at this stage."
He said there should not be any mud slinging since it was a party election.
"It is a family affair. The end result could be good."
